en: 1. Proof and refutation, along with their fallacies, are for the sake of communicating with others;
perception and inference, along with their fallacies, are for the sake of one's own understanding.
Thus is the summary of the meaning of the treatise.

2. The object intended by the proponent himself to be established is the *sādhya* (the thesis). That by which it is established is the *sādhana* (the proof). 3. The statement of the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) of the logical reason (*hetu*).
What, then, are those three characteristics?
Existence in the subject (pakṣa) alone is the first characteristic; existence only in the similar class (sapakṣa) is the second characteristic.
And the third [characteristic] is that its absence in the counter-example is ascertained.

4. In this context, the "thesis" (*pakṣa*) is a subject (*dharmin*) that is well-known, qualified by a well-known attribute (*viśeṣa*), intended by oneself to be established, and not contradicted by perception or other means of valid cognition.
For example, sound is the subject, and it is being established as qualified by the attribute of impermanence, with "because it is produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*) as the reason (*hetu*).
5. What is the similar instance (sapakṣa)? A similar instance is that which is similar by virtue of the commonality of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), such as a jar and so forth.

6. Or what is the counter-example (vipakṣa) of a reason? It is that in which the absence of the reason is stated as a necessary consequence of the absence of the probandum—for example, "such as space and so forth."
7. And this very statement of the three characteristics of the reason (hetu), when employed for the purpose of communicating to another, is called inference for others (parārthānumāna).
For example: "Sound is impermanent" is the statement of the thesis (pakṣavacana); "because it is produced" is the statement of the reason (hetuvacana);
and "like a pot, etc. is the statement of the similar instance (sapakṣavacana).
"Like space" is the statement regarding the counter-example (vipakṣa).
Furthermore, that [example] is seen to be of two kinds:
by way of similarity and by way of dissimilarity.
9. First, by way of similarity:
whatever is produced is observed to be impermanent, such as a jar and so forth.
And sound is produced.
10. Furthermore, by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya):
where there is no impermanence, there is certainly no state of being produced, as in the case of space and so forth;
yet sound is produced.
11. What, then, is a fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*)? It is that which appears like a thesis, but is not actually a thesis in its own right.
Because it is sublated by perception and the other means of valid cognition.

12. That, however, is a fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*). For example, when it is to be proven that smoke and so forth are produced by an intelligent cause which is their property-bearer (*dharmin*), a fallacious thesis contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣaviruddha*) arises.
Because smoke produced by fire is perceived through direct perception.

13. An example of that which is contradicted by inference (*anumānaviruddha*) is as follows: when it is to be proven (*sādhya*) that "the Vedic statement is the subject (*dharmin*) and is non-human-authored (*apauruṣeya*)," [it is contradicted] because the human authorship of sound is established by its being immediately following upon effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*).
14. Contradiction with one's own statement (*svavacanaviruddha*) is as follows:

the utterance "inference is not a valid means of knowledge" (*nānumānaṃ pramāṇam*), when being articulated for the purpose of communicating to another, is [itself] called inference for others (*parārtham anumāna*), because it has been stated as such.
15. An example of that which contradicts worldly consensus (*lokaviruddha*):
"A human skull is pure because it is a part of a living being, like a conch shell or mother-of-pearl."

16. An example of that which contradicts common experience (*pratītiviruddha*) is as follows: "A produced thing (*kṛtaka*) that persists for some time is impermanent. This contradicts common worldly experience, for it is universally recognized that all produced things, even those that persist for some time, are permanent.
17. An example of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*) is as follows: when a Vaiśeṣika seeks to prove to a Sāṃkhya that "sound is perishable."
18. An example of one where the subject is not established (*aprasiddhaviśeṣya*): when a Sāṃkhya attempts to prove to a Buddhist that "the self (*ātman*) is conscious."

19. An example of that which is unestablished for both [parties] is as follows: for a Vaiśeṣika, when addressing a Buddhist, [the claim] that "the self is the inherent cause of pleasure and so forth" (Htu 263).
An example of a well-known relationship is: "Wind is unstable by nature."
20. Fallacious positions have been explained.
21. What is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*)? It is that which appears to be a reason, but is not, in fact, an established reason.
22. Fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) are of three types: the unestablished (asiddha), the contradictory (viruddha), and the inconclusive (anaikāntika).
23. In that case, because it is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the subject (*pakṣa*), it is the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) known as the "unestablished" (*asiddha*).

24. That which exists neither in the subject nor in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), but exists only in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), is the fallacious reason known as the "contradictory" (*viruddha*).
Because it proves the opposite of what is to be proven.

25. In that regard, a reason (*hetu*) which exists in both the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), or does not exist in both, or is doubtful [in either case], or whose relation is unestablished (*aprasiddhasambandha*), is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) designated as "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).
This is because it fails to establish the single, definitive conclusion desired by the proponent or the opponent.
26. Unestablished for both [parties]: for example, when the impermanence of sound is to be proven, "visibility" (*cākṣuṣatva*) is a reason unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent.

27. When "trees possess consciousness" is the probandum (*sādhya*), the reason (*hetu*) "because they die when all their bark is stripped away" is unestablished for the opponent, the Buddhist; thus it is "unestablished for the opponent" (*prativādyasiddha*).
This is because the Buddhist accepts that [death] consists in the cessation of consciousness and so forth.

28. When "pleasure and so forth are insentient" is the thesis (*sādhya*), the reason (*hetu*) "because they possess origination" is unestablished for the proponent himself, the Sāṃkhya. Thus, it is [an instance of] "unestablished for the proponent" (*vādyasiddha*).

29. When a Vaiśeṣika attempts to prove to a Buddhist that "forbearance and so forth are effects of a substratum" (dharmī), the reason "because of the arising of successive similar [moments] at every moment" is unestablished for the proponent himself.
Even if the fact of arising were established, the claim that there is an arising of successive similar moments at every moment remains unestablished.
30. An example of the "unestablished in part of the subject" (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*) is as follows: "Trees are sentient because they sleep. This is the reason (*hetu*).
For a Digambara who argues as his own proponent, this is a "partially unestablished" (pakṣaikadeśāsiddha) reason;
for it is not the case that all trees possess the closing of their leaves at night.

31. Likewise, when the subject (*dharmin*) such as the earth and so forth is to be proven to be produced by an intelligent cause (*buddhimaddhetujanya*) on the grounds of the reason (*hetu*) "being an effect" (*kāryatvāt*), this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) for the Buddhist.
For the Buddhist, the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) based on perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) is not established in the case of the earth and so forth.
If it were established in the case of monasteries (*vihāra*), food, and the like, then [the reason] would be unestablished with respect to one part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*).
32. An inconclusive due to doubt (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*) is as follows: for example, when "fire is here" is the probandum (*sādhya*), because the reason itself is not certain.

33. It is also unestablished when there is doubt regarding the subject (*dharmī*), as for example: when it is to be proven that "there is a peacock in one of many groves," the reason "because of the sound of a peacock's cry" is unestablished.

34. It is also unestablished when its substratum is unestablished; for example, when "the self is omnipresent" is the thesis to be proven, the reason "because its qualities are perceived everywhere" is unestablished.
35. These ten are fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) designated as "unestablished" (asiddha).
36. What kind of fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) is said to be inconclusive (anaikāntika)?

37. For example, when a property such as the permanence of sound is to be proven, "knowability" (*prameyatva*) as a reason is a common inconclusive (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason, because it exists everywhere in both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

38. Likewise, in the case of proving the permanence of sound, the reason "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*) is an uncommon inconclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason, because it does not occur in either the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) or the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

39. Likewise, when "non-arising immediately after effort" is to be proven of sound, the reason "because of impermanence" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as it subsists in one part of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) while pervading the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

That which does not follow immediately upon effort—such as lightning, space, and so forth—is the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) for sound; in that regard, impermanence exists in some parts thereof, such as lightning, but not in [others] like space. On the other hand, everything that follows immediately upon effort, such as a jar and so forth, is the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*); in all of those cases, [impermanence] exists.

(HTU 265) 40. Likewise, when the fact that sound follows immediately upon effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is to be proven, "impermanence" (*anityatva*) is the reason (*hetu*), as it exists in all instances such as a jar and the like.
Furthermore, the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) consists of things such as lightning and space, which do not follow immediately upon effort.
In that case, it exists in one part of the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa), such as lightning and the like, but not in [other parts] such as space and the like.
Therefore, this reason, which occurs in one part of the dissimilar instances while pervading the similar instances (sapakṣa), is inconclusive (anaikāntika).

41. An inconclusive [reason] is that which occurs in only one part of both [the similar and dissimilar] classes; for example, when "eternality" is the property to be proven (sādhya) with respect to the subject (dharmin) "sound," the reason "because it is formless" (amūrtatvāt) is inconclusive.
In this case, atoms, space, and so forth constitute the similar class (sapakṣa).
In that regard, incorporeality applies to one part [of the subject], namely space, but not to atoms because atoms possess corporeality.
The pot, pleasure, and so forth constitute the counter-example (*vipakṣa*);
[the reason] exists in one part of that, namely in pleasure and so forth, but not in the pot and so forth.
42. Likewise, a reason that possesses a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) while pervading all similar instances (*sapakṣa*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as for example:

when it is to be proven (*sādhya*) that the subject (*dharmin*), such as Kapila and others, is "not omniscient," the reason (*hetu*) "because of being a speaker" exists in similar instances such as people on the street.
It is doubtful with respect to the omniscient one, who is the counter-example;
because the omniscient one is beyond the reach of the senses, it is doubtful whether such a statement exists or not.

43. Likewise, a reason whose occurrence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) is doubtful but which pervades the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For example, when it is to be proven that the subject—such as Ṛṣabha, Vardhamāna, and others—is omniscient, the reason "because of the composition of a Kevalin’s scripture" is doubtful with respect to the similar instance of an omniscient being.
Since an omniscient being is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), the composition of a Kevalin’s scripture is itself doubtful.
It exists in the counter-example, such as Varāhamihira and others who are not omniscient.
44. A reason whose positive and negative concomitance are doubtful is "inconclusive" (anaikāntika), as for example: "The living body possesses a self because it possesses breath and so forth.
It is not determined whether breath and so forth, which are associated with the living body, occur or do not occur in that which has a self or that which lacks a self.
45. Therefore, there is only the purely positive reason (*kevalānvayin*), because of the absence of a [negative] example.
46. Likewise, the second [type of] purely negative inference is: "This living body is not soulless, because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of it lacking breath and so forth.

Since there is an absence of a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*), there is neither certainty regarding positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor certainty regarding negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); thus, it is a cause of doubt.
47. These nine have been described as fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) known by the name "inconclusive" (anaikāntika).
48. What is the nature of the fallacious reason known as the contradictory (*viruddha*)?
49. For example: "Sound is the subject (dharmin); 'eternal' is the property to be proven (sādhyadharma); because it is produced (kṛtakatvāt), like space (ākāśādivat).
This reason exists only in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa), such as a jar, and not in similar instances (sapakṣa).

50. Likewise, when "sound" is the subject (*dharmin*) and "eternal" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), the reason (*hetu*) "because it follows immediately after effort" does not exist at all in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) such as space;
rather, it exists in some dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) such as a jar, but not in others such as lightning.
These two reasons prove the opposite of the essential nature of the property (*dharma*).
51. An example of a reason that proves the opposite of the specific property (*dharmaviśeṣaviparītasādhana*):

"The subject (*dharmin*) is the eye and so forth; the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is 'being for the sake of another' (*parārtha*); the reason (*hetu*) is 'because of being a composite' (*saṃghatatvāt*);
and 'like a bed, a chair, and so forth' is the statement regarding the similar instances (*sapakṣa*)."
But this reason, just as it establishes that the eyes and so forth exist for the sake of another,
likewise establishes the state of being a composite for the other; for we observe that a composite, such as a bed or a chair, provides assistance to another, such as Devadatta.

52. An example of a reason that proves the opposite of the subject's own nature (*dharmisvarūpaviparītasādhana*) is as follows: when it is to be proven that the subject (*dharmin*), such as the earth and so forth, is produced by an intelligent cause, the reason given is "because it has a substratum" (*sāśrayatvāt*).
The statement of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is "like a jar and so forth.
This reason, just as it establishes being produced by an intelligent cause, likewise establishes that the intelligent agent also has a substratum.
53. An example of a reason that proves the opposite of the specific property of the subject (*dharmin-viśeṣa-viparīta-sādhana*) is as follows:

for a Vaiśeṣika, when proving to a Mīmāṃsaka that "the self (*ātman*) is the subject [of the proposition] which possesses consciousness," the reason "because it is the locus of consciousness" proves consciousness for the self, even though the self is [according to the opponent] non-conscious. Just as [this reason] establishes consciousness [in the case of the self].
Likewise, this reason also establishes impermanence,
because consciousness is impermanent.
54. These five fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) designated as "contradictory" (viruddha) have been explained.
55. There is no such thing as a logical fallacy of the reason called *viruddhāvyabhicārī* (the "non-erroneous contradictory"); therefore, it is not appropriate to provide an example of it.
An example in that regard is as follows:
"Whatever is simultaneously connected by all things situated in every location, as well as by itself and its own relations, is omnipresent (*sarvagata*)."
"Just as space" [is the example].

And the general property (sāmānya) is connected simultaneously with all its own relata situated in every location; this is the formulation of the reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu) by Pailuka.
The second formulation belongs to Paiṭhara.
Whatever meets the conditions for perception and is not perceived in a certain place does not exist there;
for example, a jar that is absent from a particular location.
And a universal, though meeting the conditions for perception, is not perceived in the intervals between individual instances.
The non-apprehension as the reason and the previously mentioned essential nature (svabhāva) mutually sublate each other because they give rise to doubt.
Since there is no such thing as an example distinct from the similar class (sapakṣa), the similar class itself is the example by similarity (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta).
In that regard, what is a fallacious example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*)? First, by way of similarity (*sādharmya*):
"Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like action (*karman*)."
The example is deficient in the property to be proven (sādhyavikala) because action is impermanent.
59. "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like an atom. This [reason] is devoid of the probandum, because atoms are corporeal.
60. "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like a jar"—this [reason] is deficient in respect to the probandum, the probans, and both.
61. Likewise, a pseudo-example (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa) is one in which the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is doubtful.
For example: "A certain person is the subject (dharmin); he possesses passion and so forth, because he speaks; like a man on the street."
In that example, the presence of passion and so forth in the man on the street is doubtful, because the mental states of others are difficult to discern.

62. An example of a reason whose probans-property is doubtful (*saṃdigdhasādhanadharma*) is as follows: when "a certain person is subject to death" is the thesis (*sādhya*), the reason (*hetu*) "because he possesses passion and so forth" is doubtful with respect to the instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) of a man on the street.
For even one who is free from passion acts like one possessed of passion.

63. An example where both properties are doubtful (*saṃdigdhobhayadharmā dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) is as follows: when a certain person is the subject (*dharmin*) and "not being omniscient" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), and "possessing passion and so forth" is the logical reason (*hetu*).
In the case of the example of a man on the street, both the property to be proven and the means of proof are doubtful.
64. Lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*), unshown positive concomitance (*apradarśitānvaya*), and inverted positive concomitance (*viparītānvaya*) are fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).
65. In that regard, the lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) is as follows: "Whoever is a speaker possesses passion and so forth, like a man on the street.
This is because the causal relationship between being a speaker and possessing passion and so forth has been refuted.
66. An example where the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not demonstrated: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced.
Here, although the positive concomitance exists, it has not been shown by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
This is a fallacious example (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa) due to a defect in the speaker.
67. An example of inverted positive concomitance (*viparītānvaya*) is as follows:
"Whatever is impermanent is produced, like a pot, etc. Here, impermanence is the probandum (*sādhya*). One must state that the probans (*sādhana*) is pervaded by the probandum itself.
But it is not said that the probandum is pervaded by the probans;
rather, a reversed positive concomitance (*viparītānvaya*) is a fallacious example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).
68. These nine have been stated as fallacious examples by way of similarity (sādharmya).
69. Fallacious examples by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) are now stated.
70. An example that lacks the exclusion of the probandum (sādhyāvyatirekin) is as follows:
"Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like an atom."
In this case, because the atom serves as a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), the property of being a means of proof (*sādhana-dharma*), namely "immateriality," is excluded [from the example],
since atoms possess materiality; however,
the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*), namely "eternality," is not excluded.
Because the atom is eternal.
71. An example of non-exclusion from the probans (*sādhanāvyatireka*) is as follows: "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like action.
Here, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), namely eternality, is excluded [from the example], because action is non-eternal.
The property to be proven is not excluded from action, because action is incorporeal.
72. An example of that which is non-exclusive of both [the property to be proved and the reason] is as follows: "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like space.
Here, in the case of space and so forth—the example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta)—neither the property to be proved nor the reason is excluded.

73. Likewise, there are those with a doubtful exclusion of the probandum (*saṃdigdhasādhyavyatirekī*), those with a doubtful exclusion of the probans (*saṃdigdhasādhanavyatirekī*), and those with a doubtful exclusion of both (*saṃdigdhobhayavyatirekī*).
74. An example of a fallacious instance (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) with a doubtful exclusion of the probandum is as follows:
"Kapila and others are not omniscient,
because they did not compose a scripture characterized by the mark of omniscience.
This is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
"He who is omniscient taught [sciences] such as astrology, just like Ṛṣabha, Vardhamāna, and others.
In this case, there is a doubt whether the non-omniscience of Ṛṣabha, Vardhamāna, and the rest has been excluded by the example of dissimilarity (vaidharmyodāharaṇa) or not.
75. An example of a reason whose negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful is as follows:
"The person Kapila, Kaṇāda, and others are not such that their words are to be accepted by a Brahmin learned in the three Vedas, because they possess passion and other defects.

Here, the example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is: "Those whose words are to be accepted do not possess passion and other defects, just as Gautama and others, the authors of the Dharmaśāstras. [In this case,] from Gautama and others, the property of possessing passion and other defects—
The exclusion is doubtful.
76. An example of a reason where both exclusions are doubtful (*saṃdigdhobhayavyatirekī*) is as follows:
"Kapila and others are not free from passion, because they possess grasping and acquisition.
Here, the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is: "In one who is free from passion, grasping and acquisition do not occur" (Htu 270).
As in the case of Ṛṣabha, Vardhamāna, and others:

from the dissimilar instance (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) of Ṛṣabha and so forth, there arises a doubt as to whether the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma)—namely, the state of not being free from passion—is excluded from the property that serves as the reason (sādhana-dharma)—namely, the connection with possession and grasping—or not.
Possession (parigraha) is the acquisition of previously unobtained objects.
Non-abandonment of what has been obtained is "clinging" (*āgraha*).
Both of these are possible in the case of the Bull and others,
since we hear of their grasping for and clinging to the parasols, fly-whisks, and drums.

77. Non-exclusion (*avyatireka*) consists of the fallacious negative example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*), namely, the non-demonstrated exclusion (*apradarśitavyatireka*) and the inverted exclusion (*viparītavyatireka*).
78. An example of non-exclusion is as follows:
"Kapila and others are not free from passion, because they are speakers."
Where there is no state of being free from passion, there is no speaker, as in the case of a fragment of stone;
yet, even if this [person] is excluded from the fragment of stone, there remains the doubt that every person free from passion is a speaker.

79. An example where the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not demonstrated: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like space. Although this is in fact a correct example, it is a pseudo-example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) due to the fault of the speaker.
Because in an inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), the virtues and faults of the speaker are being examined.

For instance, by stating, "Whatever is eternal is necessarily seen to be unproduced, such as space and so forth," the speaker has failed to demonstrate the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) preceded by the positive pervasion (*vyāpti*) through proper analysis; thus, this is an "undemonstrated negative concomitance" (80). An example of "inverted negative concomitance" (*viparītavyatireka*) is as follows:
"That which is unconditioned is seen to be eternal.

In this case, the pervasion of the exclusion of the probandum by the exclusion of the probans must be demonstrated; therefore, it is established that wherever there is an exclusion of the probandum, there necessarily follows an exclusion of the probans.
81. Thus, the eighteen fallacious examples have been explained.
82. All these fallacies of the thesis, the reason, and the example are called "fallacious proofs" (*sādhanābhāsa*) because they fail to prove the point intended to be established by the proponent;
thus, they become faults for the proponent.
And thus, the arguments put forward by the opponent as refutations do indeed become refutations,

because they obstruct the establishment of the intended meaning of the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣavādin*). The definition of a refutation is stated separately after being analyzed as nothing other than the pointing out of deficiencies in the proof (*sādhana*).

83. Fallacious Refutation (dūṣaṇābhāsa): These very same refutations, when stated by the opponent, are called "fallacies of refutation" (jāti) when the proponent demonstrates that they are false refutations.
Because it is said that "fallacious rejoinders" (*jātyuttara*) are false refutations consisting in the pointing out of faults where no fault exists; for example,

according to the principle that "semblances of refutation" (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*) consist in pointing out a fault in a thesis when the thesis is not faulty, proclaiming a fault in a reason when the reason is faultless,
or attributing a fault to an example when the example is not faulty.

84. In this regard, the proof consisting of five members—namely, the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*)—is stated by others.
For instance: "Sound is impermanent" is the proposition; "because it is produced" is the reason;
"whatever is produced is observed to be impermanent, such as a jar and so forth" is the example.
Likewise, "sound is produced" is the application (*upanaya*);
"therefore, it is impermanent" is the conclusion (*nigamana*).
The application (*upanaya*) is that which brings the reason—capable of producing cognition in the example—to the subject (*dharmin*).
Because of the statement that "the restatement of the proposition is the conclusion," this is not so;

for the object to be proven is established by the three members themselves, known as the positive concomitance (anvaya), the negative concomitance (vyatireka), and the property of the subject (pakṣadharma).
85. For instance, at the time of debate, the formal argument must be made preceded by pervasion (*vyāpti*).
"Whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, such as a jar and so forth.
The statement of the pervasion of the probans by the probandum in the example is called positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

86. And in the case of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), the exclusion of the probans (*sādhana*) through the exclusion of the probandum (*sādhya*) is called the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); for example, "if impermanence is absent, producedness (*kṛtakatva*) is certainly not present," as in the case of space and so forth.
87. "And sound is produced" is the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
Furthermore, the thesis and the conclusion should not be stated at all.

88. Likewise, in an application characterized by similarity (sādharmya), since the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is understood through the very power of expressing the positive concomitance (anvaya), it is not stated separately.
For example: "Whatever is produced, all that should be seen as impermanent, such as a pot and so forth."
And "sound is produced"—
this is an application based on similarity (*sādharmya*).

Likewise, in an application based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), since the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is understood through the very force of the statement of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), the positive concomitance is not stated again.
Whatever is eternal is seen to be uncreated, such as space and so forth; and sound is created.
This is an argument based on dissimilarity (vaidharmya-prayoga).
89. Fallacious proofs and fallacious refutations have been explained.
90. What is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) like?
Direct perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*).
That consciousness which has gone toward or is based upon the sense faculty (*akṣa*) is direct perception.
This means that the cognitions have the five sense-faculties as their basis.

By forming a compound according to the rule *atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe dvitīyayā* (words such as *ati* and others are compounded with a word in the accusative case when they mean "surpassing" and so forth), the term *pratyakṣa* is established as being of all genders (*vācyaliṅga*).
Thus, there is "direct perception as cognition" (*pratyakṣo bodhaḥ*) and "direct perception as intellect" (*pratyakṣā buddhiḥ*).
Thus, it is established that direct knowledge is perception.
91. The five sense-faculties known as eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, and the five cognitions based upon them, are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Their corresponding objects—known as visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible object—are the five objects of cognition (*prameya*).

92. And that perception is called a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) if it is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) regarding names, universals (*jāti*), and so forth, non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*);
for it does not contradict the object as it has been shown.
93. Among these, conceptualization of names (*nāma-kalpanā*) is the cognition that "this is Devadatta";
conceptualization of universals (*jāti-kalpanā*) is the cognition that "this is a cow."
The conceptual construction that "this is the qualifier and this is the qualified" is the cognition "blue lotus.
Furthermore, any other determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) is a semblance of direct perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).
Furthermore, there is erroneous cognition regarding an object, such as the cognition of two moons by one suffering from ophthalmia,
the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, or the cognition that "this is a post" or "this is a person.
Other cognitions as well are mere semblances of perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*), because they do not lead to the attainment of the object as it was presented.
94. In that regard, perception is threefold:
with respect to conventional usage, there is sensory cognition;
and for all minds and mental factors, there is self-cognition, which is the reflexive awareness of their own nature.
And there is the yogic cognition produced from the ultimate limit of the intensification of the cultivation of the true object.

95. Its object is the particular (svalakṣaṇa); indeed, that which is capable of causal efficiency (arthakriyāsamartha) is called the particular. The universal (sāmānya), however, is not capable of causal efficiency.
96. And that alone is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that is perception (pratyakṣa).
The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) consists in the form of the apprehension of an object, and the result (phala) is likewise of that same nature;
there is no distinction whatsoever between the means of valid cognition and its result.
97. Inference is of two kinds: for oneself (*svārtha*) and for others (*parārtha*). 98. Among these, first, that which is for oneself:

when the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) has been apprehended and the relationship between the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) has been remembered, the cognizer subsequently realizes the object as it truly is by means of that; this is inference for oneself.
99. Furthermore, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is of exactly three kinds: effect (*kārya*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), and non-perception (*anupalambha*).
100. For when the relationship of cause and effect is established, the effect is to be regarded as a logical reason (*hetu*).
Just as where there is smoke, there is fire, as in the kitchen and so forth; and here there is smoke. [If fire were absent, smoke would certainly not exist, as in a watery place.]
"There is smoke here" is an essential nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*). "This is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*" is [another example].
It is like the previously established conventional usage of the term "śiṃśapā":
in the absence of tree-ness, there is simply no śiṃśapā-ness,
as in the case of a bare patch of ground.
In this case as well, once the relationship of pervaded and pervader has been ascertained, the pervaded should be regarded as the logical reason (*hetu*).
102. The reason of non-apprehension (*anupalambhahetu*) is as follows:
"There is no jar here, because it is not apprehended despite meeting the conditions for apprehension, like a rabbit's horn."
In this case as well, when the non-perception of the perceptible is ascertained as being pervaded by the absence of the perceptible, then this reason is a prover.
103. What is a fallacy of inference? It is of two kinds: *pūrvavat* (based on what precedes) and *śeṣavat* (based on what remains).
Furthermore, all forms of inference postulated by others, such as that which is "based on general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), are merely fallacious inferences (*anumānābhāsa*).

Because among those [things], there is an absence of a necessary connection characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from that (*tadutpatti*), the relationship of probandum and probans exists only when a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) or a pervaded-pervader relationship (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) is established, and not otherwise,
since deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is possible.
104. For example, one might say, "This cloud will surely rain because it has a deep sound";
yet, even for a cloud with a deep sound, there is the possibility that its rain may be obstructed.
105. Just as it is known that rain has fallen above from the sight of a river's flood, even by the sight of the river's flood through such signs as the breaking of its banks.
106. Just as these grains of rice are cooked because they are contained within the same vessel, like the rice that has already been seen [to be cooked].
107. "These fruits are ripe because they are attached to the same branch, like a fruit that has already been consumed.
In this case, even if [the reason] is observed repeatedly, there remains the very possibility of a deviation (vyabhicāra) between the probandum and the probans.
108. Just as it is observed that whatever is earthen is all scratchable by iron—
such as wood and so forth—
even a diamond is earthen.
109. Whatever possesses breath is all possessed of a neck;
for example, from the young camel onwards, even the crab is a living being.

110. Just as it is observed that whatever substance is liquid is moistening, such as water, and mercury is also a liquid substance; in this way, other fallacious inferences (anumānābhāsa) are also to be understood.
The Instruction on the Reality of Causes is completed.
